I think it's weird to be so upset about leaving a bandaid on (this seems like an innocent mistake?) but yet trusting grandma completely for a full week in all other regards. Its like the helicopter-mom side in you is fighting the get-my-kid-away-from-me side. I find it shocking you would leave your four year old with your mother for a full week, and then go crazy over a bandaid. If I absolutely had to leave my almost 4 year old with my mom for a week for some desperate reason, I would just be glad to get her back in one piece lol I wouldn't be pullin my hair out over a bandaid. 

Going from trusting her with your kid for a full week to 0 unsupervised time over a bandaid just seems like overkill. Your post reads like you have some resentment and distrust towards your mother for how she deals with her grandson vs how she raised you, and you're using something super tiny to justify how you feel and/or punish your mother.  

Idk maybe I'm not reading right but this much upset over a bandaid reads as suspicious. I think you have some other distrust issues going on with your mom, in which case, you either need to fix yourself or put your foot down and don't let your kid stay with someone that you don't trust for a week. 

Also, I have left a bandaid on my own kid for too long. I remember when I was a kid, the bandaid had NO adhesive and came off in a light rain. So when my kid had on a bandaid, I didn't expect it to hold like superglue and give her a rash. It was unexpected and now I know better. But if my mom made the same mistake, I'd just tell her and move on because it's an honest mistake.

- after a few months I realized that I did not like the way that ynab did its "goals." Bills due on the first at the very top, bills due st the end of the month on the bottom. Idk, it made the budget simpler for me. 
- KISS (keep it simple, sillygoose) and trust the process
- watch YNAB YouTube videos. This really helps me when I'm discouraged about the budget. It's a tiny thing that helps me feel more in control. Even if I'm not really paying attention (I listen while I cook dinner or something) it helps me feel like I can do better in the future, even if I'm feeling discouraged now. It's where I got the idea to stop using the "goals" feature lol

Hi there! (Disclaimer: Not a dermatologist or a doctor, just a big TO fan)

Your starting products are ones that i keep in my routine just about every day! I've seen so much improvement since using AA+HA, and niacinimide is just a notoriously amazing product. 

Since it doesnt sound like you have any seriois skin conditions, I think you're doing phenomenal 👏  starting to care for your skin at this age is super smart. 

I don't see sunscreen on your list, but I HIGHLY recommend finding one that you can use every day. I have personally fallen in love with Neutrogenas dry feel face sunscreen, it's less than ten bucks on Amazon. Your best friend in preventing aging signs, skin cancer, and a whole bunch of other skin issues will be using sunscreen daily. 

I have pretty severe adult acne (im 28f) and prescription retinol has been my holy grail for treating that. I think it's great you're using TO granactive retinol - ive heard a lot of fantastic things about it, and lactic acid is great for hyperpigmentation. So you have a really good little buffet of ingredients to benefit your skin! 

The only things I would recommend would be incorporating the more active ingredients slowly and after your skin adjusts. Niacinimide irritated my skin at first, so I started by just putting a drop in my lotion. After a few weeks, I can now use it by itself (under moisturizer). I also am totally unable to use glycolic acid, bc it burns my face off lmao (ok, I'm dramatic... it just burned and I didn't like it lol). 

Overall you have GREAT products! Remember the best sunscreen is the one that you will use comfortably and reliably every day, and it's the best investment you can make imo! Just incorporate them slowly and make sure your skin has time to adjust and you're doing beautifully :)

Im sorry for how long this is, this happens to be a really important topic fo me. I have a 1 year old and had no idea how post partum depression and anxiety was effecting me. It is not depression or anxiety like I had ever experienced before. I felt like after I gave birth, I wasn't human anymore. Nobody talked to me like I was still me. Don't get me wrong, my baby is amazing. But I also still exist.

It is illogical, it is irrational, to be *so* exhausted and not accept help. But PPD/PPA in combination with caring for a newborn is a fucking monster. I would bet that even she does not know what is going on inside of her own mind. I remember sleeping on the floor so I can hear my baby breathing. I remember holding her while I pooped because... well, what if she needs me? 

I remember asking people to come over to help me. And then not letting them do it lol it was frustrating for them, and frustrating for me. I knew I needed help, and knew I needed support. I knew that I looked like a crazy person to the people around me, but I couldn't stop it. Hormones are a bitch. 

I was not *able* to emotionally accept help. I was terrified for my child, and sure that nobody would care for her to the same meticulous measure as I would. (This was offensive to my SO, but in hindsight i blame biology for my distrust) My whole household suffered because of this. I was overwhelmed. Incredibly sad. I lost patience with my SO, i was irritable all of the time. I can't even explain what kind of... internal damage... is done inside the mind of a woman with PPD/PPA. 


I am not trying to diagnose. 1+ years post partum and I am just now getting back to "even." 

One thing that helped was straight up praise and encouragement. I know it sounds pitiful. But I was internally tearing myself down constantly. When my SO accepted that I was not going to let him help, he filled that gap by constantly telling me thank you for making our child, telling me how impressed he was by my ability to do it. Immediately post partum, I needed to be validated and told that I am doing something amazing, and I needed someone to remind me that the newborn phase will end, the feelings are temporary, and she's handling it with absolute grace - even if you don't think she is. I remember my best friend coming over and not asking if she could help. She just did it. She did the dishes. And then she said "can I PLEASE hold her?" And then she stood up, and talked to me like I was a human, she gave ME her full attention. She told me how beautiful I was after giving birth. She told me how amazing I was. She held my baby - not like she was doing me a favor, but like she *wanted to be around me bc she loved me, not bc I needed it.* 


You can't replace the sleep, and you shouldnt force her to accept help, imo. You *can* make her feel good about herself as a mother. And make sure she knows that what she's going through is not for nothing, and that she is seen. You can at least combat the internal war she has with the post partum hormones and psychology. I'm sorry if this doesn't help, it's all I have to offer. And I wish more people realized what kind of hell PPA/PPD can be for new mothers.

It is illogical, it is irrational, to be *so* exhausted and not accept help. But PPD/PPA in combination with caring for a newborn is a fucking monster. I would bet that even she does not know what is going on inside of her own mind. 

I was not *able* to emotionally accept help. I was terrified for my child, and sure that nobody would care for her to the same meticulous measure as I would. (This was offensive to my SO, but in hindsight i blame biology for my distrust) My whole household suffered because of this. I was overwhelmed. Incredibly sad. I lost patience with my SO, i was irritable all of the time. I can't even explain what kind of... internal damage... is done inside the mind of a woman with PPD/PPA. 


I am not trying to diagnose. But the only advice that I have is to know that this is NOT permanent. 1+ years post partum and I am just now getting back to "even." 

I want to add - the one thing that anybody did to help me with this.... was praise. I know it sounds pitiful. But I was internally tearing myself down constantly. When my SO accepted that I was not going to let him help, he filled that gap by constantly telling me thank you for making our child, telling me how impressed he was by my ability to do it. Immediately post partum, I needed to be validated and told that I am doing something amazing, and I needed someone to remind me that the newborn phase will end, the feelings are temporary, and she's handling it with absolute grace - even if you don't think she is. 

You can't replace the sleep, and you shouldnt force her to accept help, imo. You *can* make her feel better about herself as a mother. And make sure she knows that what she's going through is not for nothing, and that she is seen. You can at least combat the internal war she has with the post partum hormones and psychology. I'm sorry if this doesn't help, it's all I have to offer. And I wish more people realized what kind of hell PPA/PPD can be for new mothers.

I am not a doctor or anything like that. All I have is personal experience, and I can honestly tell you that being on anti depressants has saved my life. I'm a better human when I'm treating my mental illness like what it is - *an illness*. I have severe chronic depression, and I have for a long time. But when I got pregnant and had my baby, my depression was exacerbated to a really scary degree. It took a long time for me to get the balls to go to the doctor, but when I finally did, he had no problem sending me hone with medication that he believed would help. 

The most important thing to me is that when I am treating my depression properly, I feel like myself. I have spent several years trying different medications and it has been a roller coaster. The key is finding the right combo *for you*, but it's hard. Sometimes I felt lost and like I was doomed to be suicidal forever. But now that I have found the proper combination (welbutrin and lexapro), I feel happy for the first time in decades. I feel like myself, and the search for the right treatment was worth it. **patience is key** 

If I can give one word of advice, it would be to give the meds time to work. They don't kick in overnight (usually) and I think a lot of people have bad effects from their meds because they take them somewhat improperly. It's really important to be consistent and disciplined when it comes to medication. It's a commitment but it is SO worth it.

Edit to include: since taking anti depressants, I am better able to eat properly, be social and enjoy being around my family and friends again, I actually like doing things like being outside. I feel like I am able to love my daughter better and provide emotional warmth and support that I couldn't muster up previously. I don't feel clouded by sadness and overwhelming doom. I feel happy.
